papers.title_in_file: Training variational quantum algorithms is NP-hard
papers.version_note: arXiv:2101.07267v2, 14 Apr 2022 (the published-revision text). The text layer prints the not-equal sign of 'P != NP' as 'P = NP' throughout; the rendered page 1 shows the abstract with the not-equal sign.
sections_read: A. VQA optimization with quantum computer access
B. Logarithmic number of qubits - polynomial Hilbert space dimension
C. Quantum approximate optimization algorithms for a logarithmic number of qubits

figures.shows: A sketch of a VQA routine: a quantum circuit on four qubits, each starting in |0>, with parametrized blocks U1(phi1) to U5(phi5) and a block UM, ending in measurements; the measured results go to a Post Processing box, which passes <O(phi)> to a Classical Optimization box (drawn in red) that feeds updated parameters back to the circuit and outputs phi_guess and phi_final.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 1 illustrates a possible VQA routine.

papers.what_it_is: A theory paper proving that classical training of variational quantum algorithms (VQE and QAOA settings) is NP-hard, also for logarithmically many qubits and free fermions, by reduction from MaxCut.

assertions.value: The authors state that the classical optimization problems corresponding to variational quantum eigensolvers and quantum approximate optimization algorithms are NP-hard.
quotes: We show that the corresponding classical optimization problems are NP-hard.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract summarizes results that the paper proves in later theorems; this entry is the summary, not a statement of conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that the hardness is robust: for every polynomial time algorithm there are instances for which the relative error from the classical optimization problem can be arbitrarily large, assuming P is not equal to NP.
quotes: Moreover, the hardness is robust in the sense that, for every polynomial time algorithm, there are instances for which the relative error resulting from the classical optimization problem can be arbitrarily large assuming P = NP.
assertions.certainty_reason: Abstract summary; the proved form is Corollary 1.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the not-equal sign as an equals sign; the rendered page 1 shows 'P not equal to NP'. The value follows the rendered page.

assertions.value: The authors state that, even for classically tractable systems composed of only logarithmically many qubits or free fermions, they show the optimization to be NP-hard.

assertions.certainty_reason: Abstract summary of Theorem 1, Theorem 2 and Theorem 5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the training landscape can have many far from optimal persistent local minima, and that gradient and higher order descent algorithms will generally converge to far from optimal solutions.
quotes: Our analysis shows that the training landscape can have many far from optimal persistent local minima.
This means that gradient and higher order descent algorithms will generally converge to far from optimal solutions.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement in the abstract; the paper proves a bound only for the constructed instances.

assertions.value: The authors state that persistent local minima can render the training of VQAs infeasible, and that they encode the NP-hard MaxCut problem into the classical optimization task for several versions of VQAs, which have many far from optimal local minima.
